title: Signett
pitch: Signett is an open-source TypeScript toolkit for building reliable, observable, and testable WebMCP applications.
about_excerpt: Signett is an open-source TypeScript toolkit for building reliable, observable, and testable WebMCP applications. Like 1 Comment Story Updates What is Signett Signett is a reliability and evaluation layer for production WebMCP applications. In our live Saleor demo , an agent discovers catalog and checkout tools, finds a product, requests human approval, and submits a purchase request. What makes it special is that the storefront updates only after the purchase is verifiably complete, as provided by Signett. We also simulate a browser response loss after the mutation commits and show how Signett recovers the authoritative result instead of creating a duplicate. What it does WebMCP gives agents a structured way to use website capabilities. Signett adds the execution semantics and developer workflow needed to operate those capabilities reliably. The Signett SDK accomplishes that through several core features: JSON Schema validation before application code runs trusted application context and application-owned authorization human confirmation for consequential effects idempotency and replay coordination operation journaling and ambiguous-failure recovery authoritative postcondition verification cancellation and structured repair guidance privacy-conscious OpenTelemetry traces React bindings for verified UI updates deterministic testing without a model or browser Simple read tools remain lightweight. Consequential tools can use the complete guarded lifecycle. Signett does not replace WebMCP, authentication, backend transaction guarantees, or application business logic. The website continues to own identity, policy, state, consent UI, and every backend effect. Signett creates a structured boundary around those existing capabilities. The wider project includes the TypeScript SDK, a Chrome side-panel agent, a headless evaluation CLI, a local Inspector, OpenTelemetry export, reference applications, reproducible benchmarks, and reviewed evidence. Inspiration - Why Do We Need This? I am a strong believer that the web will be largely agentic in a few years. While we have seen a lot of promise with browser-use agents, what bothered me the most was that these harnesses were trying to operate on websites built for humans, clicking buttons, while they should be using tools/MCPs. Then, I discovered WebMCP and was instantly excited. However, I quickly found that while the protocol is extremely valuable, a real developer trying to make their websites agentic doesn't have an ecosystem built around it. Specifically, I saw several problems: What happens when an agent retries a purchase? What if the backend commits an effect but the response disappears? How does the user retain control over consequential actions? When should the UI update? How does a developer test the interface repeatedly, inspect traces, or detect a regression? These are familiar distributed-systems problems, but agentic websites make them more common and more consequential. Signett was built to answer a specific question: How do we move from “an agent can call this tool” to “an agent can perform this action safely, predictably, and verifiably”? That idea became Signett. How we built it Signett is a TypeScript monorepo with four primary layers. Signett SDK createSignett() creates a WebMCP-facing application surface. signett.expose() compiles the tool’s schema and registers it through the native document.modelContext.registerTool() API. Each tool defines its agent-facing contract and existing application function. Optional hooks add context, authorization, confirmation, idempotency, recovery, verification, output budgets, and lifecycle observation. Signett Chrome Agent The Chrome side-panel agent discovers and invokes only the WebMCP tools exposed by the active page. It deliberately has no DOM or screenshot fallback, so missing or poorly designed capabilities remain visible to developers. Signett Eval The CLI opens the real application in headless Chrome, discovers its live WebMCP inventory, runs saved tasks, and records bounded evidence. Applications can provide their own reset, snapshot, and grading hooks. This means success can be determined from the database or domain model rather than from the agent’s final response. signett check compares evaluation results against a reviewed baseline and can detect regressions in task success, safety, capability discovery, tool selection, argument validity, latency, token usage, and trial coverage. Observability and benchmarks Signett emits lifecycle events covering validation, authorization, confirmation, execution, replay or recovery, output measurement, and verification. These can power an in-page Inspector or be exported as OTLP/HTTP JSON to systems such as Jaeger. Inputs, outputs, application context, error messages, and stack traces are excluded by default. The repository also includes deterministic safety tests, real-agent evaluations, reference integrations, benchmark methodology, and reviewed evidence. Challenges we ran into One of the hardest problems was defining correct behavior after an ambiguous failure: a server may successfully commit an order or payment while the response is lost. Blindly retrying could duplicate the action, but blindly reporting failure would also be incorrect. Signett combines durable idempotency records, operation journals, recovery logic, and authoritative state verification to handle this case explicitly. Authorization and idempotency also interact in subtle ways. Returning a cached result must never bypass a current permission check. Signett therefore reevaluates authorization before every idempotency lookup, including replays. Another challenge was making observability useful without turning it into a privacy risk. Signett records lifecycle metadata and timing information by default, while avoiding tool inputs, outputs, application context, and stack traces unless the application explicitly chooses otherwise. Building high-quality benchmarks to hill-climb on was hard, but I think we got a lot of good-quality evaluations. Check out the benchmarks folder in the open-source repository. Finally, WebMCP is still experimental and evolving. I had to design useful abstractions without hiding the native API or prematurely inventing a competing protocol. Accomplishments that we're proud of Signett became more than a wrapper around tool registration. It now supports an end-to-end developer loop: Expose a native WebMCP capability. Inspect and invoke it in Chrome. Test its execution invariants deterministically. Exercise it with a real model in headless Chrome. Grade the result against the authoritative application state. Inspect its lifecycle through OpenTelemetry. Compare the run with a reviewed baseline. The same live WebMCP tools power the browser agent, the application UI, deterministic tests, and headless evaluations. There is no parallel demo-only tool catalog.
